title: Théorie arithmétique. Théorie de Galois des motifs (1965) : notes manuscites (s.d.), tapuscrit (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Setting: M is a semisimple 'motivic' (Tannakian) category over Q. It is described by its gerbe 𝒢 of fibre functors with lien (band) L, following Giraud's language of gerbes and bands.

Hypothesis: L is of multiplicative type, so in particular commutative. A commutative band is canonically globalised by a group over the base, so L comes from an algebraic group G over Q of multiplicative type. Hence G^0 is a torus.

Step 1. Let E be a 'faithful' motive, i.e. a tensor generator, so that G acts faithfully on (any fibre of) E. Because the band is commutative, G acts on every object as an automorphism of the identity functor. E is viewed as a section of the fibred category HOM(𝒢, Vect/Proj) of representations of the gerbe. In particular each u in G(Q) gives an automorphism φ(u) of E in M, so we get φ : G(Q) → End_M(E).

Step 2. Choose a polarisation form ψ : E⊗E → Q(-w) on E. This makes A = End_M(E) a 'Riemann algebra': a finite-dimensional semisimple Q-algebra with a positive (Rosati-type) involution a ↦ a'. Since ψ is a morphism of M, it is G-equivariant, with G acting on the Tate object Q(-w) through a character ε : G → G_m (weight/similitude character). Hence φ(u)φ(u)' = ε(u)·1 for u in G(Q).

Step 3. For u in U = Ker ε we get φ(u)φ(u)' = id. So the subalgebra generated by the φ(u) is stable under the involution, and U(Q) lies in the 'unitary group' {a : aa' = 1} of A. Because the involution is positive, the real points of this unitary group form a compact Lie group. Since U^0(Q) is Zariski dense in U^0 and φ is faithful, U^0 lies inside this unitary group. Conclusion: U^0 is a torus whose real points are compact, i.e. an R-anisotropic torus.

Purpose: this is the structural lemma behind 'abelian (commutative) motivic Galois group ⇒ CM-type behaviour'. The weight character splits off, and the kernel of the weight is an R-anisotropic torus. That is exactly the defining property of the Serre group / Mumford–Tate tori of polarisable CM Hodge structures, and of the connected Taniyama group.
errors: If the faithful motive E is not pure, a single polarisation form of one weight does not exist. One must work weight by weight, so ε is really a family of weight characters, or reduce to a pure E. The page tacitly assumes E is pure.

The passage from 'U(Q) lies in the unitary group' to 'U^0 is compact' needs the Zariski-density / closure argument and faithfulness of φ. The phrase 'Or un groupe U^0 est donc compact' compresses this step; it is correct once supplied.
Compatibility of the polarisation with the G-action, i.e. that ψ is a morphism in M with G acting on the Tate object by ε, is used implicitly.
'G^0 compact' should be read as 'G^0(R) compact', i.e. anisotropic over R.

ideas.what: Describing a Tannakian (motivic) category by its gerbe of fibre functors and its band; a commutative band descends to an actual group G over Q acting on every object.
ideas.modern_name: Tannakian gerbe / band of a Tannakian category; commutative case gives a group over the base
ideas.where_published: Ideas of Grothendieck developed in Saavedra Rivano, 'Catégories tannakiennes' (LNM 265)

ideas.what: A polarisation on a motive turns End_M(E) into a semisimple algebra with positive involution ('algèbre de Riemann').
ideas.modern_name: Rosati involution / positivity of polarisations in Tannakian categories
ideas.usually_credited_to: Weil/Rosati classically for abelian varieties; Saavedra Rivano and Deligne for polarised Tannakian categories
ideas.where_published: Related to the standard conjectures (Grothendieck 1968/69, 'Standard conjectures on algebraic cycles'), where positivity (Hodge standard conjecture) gives a positive involution

ideas.what: If the motivic Galois group is of multiplicative type, then the identity component of the kernel of the weight character is a torus with compact real points (R-anisotropic).
ideas.modern_name: Serre's condition: Serre group / Mumford–Tate torus of polarisable CM Hodge structures; ker(weight)^0 anisotropic over R; connected Taniyama group
ideas.usually_credited_to: Serre (Abelian l-adic representations, 1968), Deligne (Motifs et groupes de Taniyama, 1982), Langlands; Milne's expositions

missed.claim: In notes dated (at least in part) 1965, Grothendieck already argues inside a gerbe-theoretic Tannakian framework. Using the positivity of polarisations, he proves that for a commutative motivic Galois group the weight kernel's identity component is a compact torus. This anticipates the Serre-group condition and the polarised-Tannakian machinery later credited to Serre (1968), Saavedra (1972) and Deligne (1982). The result itself is now standard; what is undocumented is the historical priority and the specific 'algèbre de Riemann' argument.
missed.quote: Choisissons une forme de polarisation sur E, d'où une structure d'algèbre de Riemann sur A = End_M(E) ... On trouve que U^0 est un tore compact.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Mainly historical: it documents Grothendieck's own route to the CM/Serre-group structure of abelian motives via polarisations. It is not a new mathematical result. The dating of the archival unit spans 1965 to about 1977, so priority is uncertain.

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is correct and now standard: polarisations imply that the weight kernel of an abelian motivic group is R-anisotropic. The interest is historical, since it shows Grothendieck early on with gerbes, bands and Rosati positivity, prefiguring Serre/Deligne/Saavedra. There is no new result for specialists, and the dating is uncertain.
transcription_corrections: Top insertion 'semi-simple [?]': the handwriting reads '½ simples', i.e. 'semi-simples' (a correct reading).

The insertion above 'groupe algébrique' marked 'commutatif [?]' is not clearly visible; the inserted phrase is 'non de type multiplicatif' / 'de type multiplicatif' attached to 'commutatif'. More precisely: 'est [commutatif] {non: de type multiplicatif}, donc correspond à un groupe algébrique G sur Q'.
'HOM(𝒢, Proj[?])': the last word is hard to read. It could be 'Vect' or an abbreviation for projective modules; it is uncertain.
'Or un groupe {U^0 est} donc compact' is better read as 'Or ce groupe est compact; donc U^0 est compact' (roughly).
The overline insertion 'd'une forme réelle [?] / Q' is more plausibly 'formé des éléments [de A réels / Q]'; the reading is uncertain.
The crossed-out line reads 'Soit U = Ker(G^0 → G_m), dont U opère' (struck).
